design_detail: Narrative review of the clinical pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of ketamine in anaesthesia and pain therapy, written by four anaesthesiologists and clinical pharmacologists for a pharmacokinetics journal. One database (PubMed Medline) was searched to 2 February 2016 with eight listed keywords, limited to English-language papers in peer-reviewed journals; further papers were taken from review articles and from the bibliographies of relevant papers, titles were screened for relevance by the authors, and data were extracted after what the authors call critical examination. No eligibility criteria, no counts of records found, screened or included, no duplicate screening, no appraisal of the included studies and no quantitative synthesis. The review has 159 references, one large table collecting pharmacokinetic parameters by route and formulation from fourteen primary studies, two figures redrawing the drug-interaction results of five studies by the authors' own group, and sections on mechanism, perioperative and chronic-pain use, depression, formulations by route, and side effects.
can_establish: What the anaesthesia and pain literature to February 2016 reported about ketamine's absorption by route, its metabolism by cytochrome P450 enzymes, its interactions with inhibitors and inducers of those enzymes, the plasma concentrations associated with loss of consciousness and with experimental analgesia, and the state of the clinical evidence in perioperative care, chronic pain, cancer pain and depression, with the primary studies named so that each figure can be traced.
cannot_establish: Whether the evidence summarized is complete or representative (one database, English only, no eligibility criteria and no record counts); the quality of any cited study, none of which is appraised; any pooled estimate or interval; the frequency of any adverse effect; and anything about the harms of non-medical ketamine use or about deaths, which the review covers in a single short section.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence base is whatever the authors retrieved from PubMed Medline up to 2 February 2016, plus papers found in review articles and in the bibliographies of retrieved papers; no number of records found, screened, excluded or included is given (p. 3 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: English-language papers in peer-reviewed journals; beyond that, relevance to the aim of the review as judged by the authors, with no stated criteria and no second screener (p. 3 of the online-first PDF).
sample.selection_effects: One database, one language and selection by the authors' own judgement, so what was left out cannot be seen. The review's frame is anaesthesia and pain therapy, and the human pharmacokinetic table is built from small studies, several with three to eight participants, including six from the authors' own group on oral S-ketamine and its interactions. The sections on perioperative and chronic-pain use cite systematic reviews, while the section on long-term harm rests on four sources.

exposure.measurement: Varies across the cited studies and is not described: Table 1 gives route, nominal amount, sample size and the parameters, but not the analytical method, and the review does not say which rows come from stereoselective assays, although it reports separate values for S-ketamine and the racemate throughout.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported as study conditions in Table 1: single intravenous, intramuscular, oral, sublingual, rectal and intranasal administration and short infusions of racemic ketamine or S-ketamine, in healthy volunteers and in patients with neuropathic pain, with sample sizes of 3 to 12 per row (pp. 4-5 of the online-first PDF). The review also prints clinical anaesthetic and analgesic dosing schemes and definitions of low-dose use; these are the review's clinical recommendations for practitioners and are not reproduced in this card.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the cited pharmacokinetic studies. Combinations are covered only as pharmacokinetic interactions with cytochrome P450 inhibitors and inducers (clarithromycin, grapefruit juice, ticlopidine, itraconazole, rifampicin, St John's wort) and as the clinical co-administration of sedatives to attenuate psychotomimetic effects; combinations used outside medicine are not discussed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable: the review compares routes and formulations with intravenous administration as each cited study did, and compares S-ketamine with racemic ketamine and with R-ketamine.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the review reports no primary data of its own.

outcomes.instruments: Pharmacokinetic parameters as the cited studies reported them (peak concentration, area under the curve, time to peak, elimination half-life, bioavailability), collected in Table 1; cytochrome P450 interaction effects as the mean percentage change in area and peak concentration with 95% confidence intervals, redrawn in Figures 3 and 4 from five studies by the authors' group, with no numerical values printed; effective concentrations for loss and return of consciousness and for experimental analgesia taken from cited studies; clinical outcomes as the cited trials and systematic reviews reported them.
outcomes.validity_norms: The review does not say how it chose which figures to carry forward, and the footnotes to Table 1 show that the entries mix means with standard errors, means with standard deviations, medians with ranges and medians with interquartile ranges, and areas integrated over different windows, within the same columns (pp. 4-5 of the online-first PDF).
outcomes.operationalization: Bioavailability is reported as each cited study computed it, against that study's own intravenous reference. Harm is not operationalized: the side-effects section lists reported adverse effects without frequencies, denominators or exposure durations.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no synthesis, no pooling and no statistical testing of the review's own.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reported as cited, with no synthesis. Disposition: alpha half-life 2-4 minutes and beta half-life 2-4 hours; plasma protein binding 10-30%; steady-state volume of distribution 160-550 L per 70 kg; systemic clearance 60-147 L/h per 70 kg; about 80% of ketamine N-demethylated to norketamine, measurable in plasma 2-3 minutes after an intravenous bolus with a peak at 30-60 minutes (pp. 3, 7 of the online-first PDF). Bioavailability by route: 8-24% by mouth overall, with 17-24% for racemic ketamine and 8-11% for S-ketamine; 24-30% sublingual; about 30% rectal; about 45% nasal; about 93% intramuscular (pp. 2, 12-14 of the online-first PDF). Concentration-effect: effective concentrations for loss of consciousness 241 ng/mL (SD 90) for the racemate and 111 (SD 30) for S-ketamine, and for return of consciousness 148 (SD 46) and 75 (SD 21), taken from a textbook chapter; psychedelic effects reported from about 50 ng/mL with intensity increasing linearly between 50 and 200 ng/mL; experimental analgesia above 100-160 ng/mL after intravenous racemate and at about 40 ng/mL after oral dosing (p. 9 of the online-first PDF). Enantiomers: clearance of S-ketamine given alone 26.3 mL/min/kg against 14.8 for racemic ketamine, and 18.5 for the S-enantiomer within the racemate, in ten healthy men (p. 7 of the online-first PDF). Clinical: perioperative low-dose ketamine reported to reduce opioid consumption by 40%; two systematic reviews found no reduction in chronic postsurgical pain overall, but restricting to intravenous administration the relative risk fell by 25% (number needed to treat 12) at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; subcutaneous ketamine added to opioids in 185 patients with cancer pain did not reduce pain scores against placebo; an anaesthetic amount of S-ketamine raised whole-brain cerebral blood flow by 36% and a subanaesthetic amount by 13% (pp. 10-12 of the online-first PDF). Interaction magnitudes appear only as figures without numbers.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; the review is not described as systematic and follows no reporting guideline.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 leaves the bioavailability column empty for every row taken from the three-person formulation study (Yanagihara et al., 2003), although the text cites that same study for the rectal figure of about 30% and the nasal figure of about 45%, which the source does print. The interaction results are shown only as figures, so the magnitudes and intervals cannot be read. Sample sizes appear in Table 1 but are never carried into the text, the Key Points or the abstract, where the bioavailability figures are stated as properties of the drug. The side-effects section runs to one short section with five references and gives no frequency for any adverse effect.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative summary in which the primary studies are named and tabulated: oral bioavailability of ketamine is low and highly variable because of first-pass metabolism by CYP3A and CYP2B6; inhibitors and inducers of those enzymes change exposure to oral S-ketamine substantially; sublingual, rectal and especially nasal administration give higher systemic availability and less norketamine than swallowing; concentrations associated with loss of consciousness, psychedelic effects and experimental analgesia differ by about an order of magnitude; and in clinical use the evidence is strongest for perioperative opioid sparing and weakest for long-term analgesia in chronic pain and for cancer pain. The table shows that most of the route figures come from studies of three to twelve people.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The route figures are stated without their sample sizes or sources wherever they are given as numbers (the Introduction on p. 2, Sections 7.2 and 7.5 on pp. 12-13 and the Summary on p. 14), so that oral bioavailability of 8-24% and nasal bioavailability of about 45% read as constants of the drug rather than as results from small studies, the nasal figure resting on three people; the Abstract and the Key Points make the same point without a figure. Section 7.3 attaches the intramuscular bioavailability of about 93% to an intramuscular dose of 2-4 mg/kg, whereas the study cited for it that I have read gave 0.5 mg/kg and computed 93% from four participants. The Summary states that S-ketamine is a two times more effective anaesthetic and analgesic than the racemate, where the abstract says this has been postulated. The side-effects section states that because ketamine raises blood pressure and heart rate and preserves respiratory activity a lethal overdose is unlikely, with no citation and no mortality data, in a review whose sources on long-term harm are a survey of urinary symptoms, a review of cystitis, a diffusion-imaging study and a pharmacy update; the same section calls the long-term safety profile unclear.

timeline.event: Bioavailability and kinetics of intravenous, intramuscular and oral ketamine in healthy volunteers; the source of the intramuscular figure of about 93% and the oral figure of about 17% that this review carries, from four people per route
Plasma profiles after five racemic preparations in three healthy Japanese men; the source of this review's sublingual, rectal and nasal figures
Review of ketamine use for the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs, covering the non-medical-use, bladder and cognitive literature that this review treats in one short section
Absolute bioavailability of racemic ketamine from a sublingual formulation in eight healthy volunteers (Rolan et al.), tabulated here at 29%

Population pharmacokinetics of S-ketamine and norketamine after intravenous and oral dosing (Fanta et al.), cited here for steady state after the third dose and for the estimate that a 2.4 times larger oral amount is needed to match intravenous exposure

replication.where_it_stands: The review is a pointer to primary studies, not an independent source of data. For every route-by-route figure the encyclopedia should cite the primary study that Table 1 names, with its sample size; the review's own contribution is the collection, the account of cytochrome P450 interactions from its authors' trials, and its judgements about where the clinical evidence was insufficient as of February 2016. Its treatment of long-term harm was already thin relative to the urological and cohort literature published between 2007 and 2014 and says nothing about deaths.

funding.funder: No funding was received for the conduct of this study (Compliance with Ethical Standards, p. 14 of the online-first PDF).
funding.declared_conflicts: The four authors state that they have no conflicts of interest directly relevant to the content of this study (p. 14 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Turku and Turku University Hospital, and University of Helsinki and Helsinki University Hospital. Five of the drug-interaction studies that the review summarizes in Table 1 and redraws in Figures 3 and 4 are the authors' own, and the review's conclusions about the metabolism and interactions of oral S-ketamine follow from them. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a registered protocol, several databases, no language limit, duplicate screening and extraction, and formal appraisal of the pharmacokinetic studies, reporting every bioavailability figure with its sample size, its assay and an interval; and, separately, a systematic review of the harms of repeated and long-term ketamine exposure that includes the bladder, cognitive, dependence and mortality literature, which this review's frame excludes.

domains.note: More than most narrative reviews: one named database, a stated last-search date (2 February 2016) and eight listed keywords, with papers added from reviews and bibliographies. But one database only, English only, no eligibility criteria, no counts of records found or included, no second screener, and selection by the authors' judgement of relevance, so what was omitted cannot be seen.

No formal appraisal of any study, and Table 1's rows carry no caveat about their sample sizes in the text. Methodological weakness is nevertheless named in several places: the pharmacometric models are called preliminary and to be interpreted cautiously, the evidence on intracranial pressure is reported as graded C with severe methodological limitations, both complex regional pain syndrome trials are said to have methodological shortcomings, and one of them is noted as stopped halfway.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The section on cytochrome P450 interactions and both of its figures rest on five studies by this group, and the review's conclusions about oral S-ketamine follow from them. The rest of the review draws on a wide literature.

The review generally marks uncertainty, saying that the optimal route and duration are yet to be established, that preliminary results should be interpreted carefully, and that the long-term safety profile is unclear. Against that, it states without any citation that ketamine's cardiovascular and respiratory profile makes a lethal overdose unlikely, and prints clinical dosing schemes without the dose-finding evidence behind them.

domains.domain: Balance of clinical benefits against harms (non-medical use, deaths and long-term bladder and cognitive damage under-represented)
domains.note: Eleven sections cover mechanism, anaesthesia, analgesia, special patient groups, chronic pain, depression and formulations; harm is one short section with five references, which names cystitis, bladder changes, cognitive disturbances, psychological dependence, hepatic dysfunction and hypersalivation without a single frequency, and the review states that a lethal overdose is unlikely without engaging any mortality literature. The frame is the clinical use of ketamine by anaesthetists, and the harms of repeated use are outside it.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used. The search is better documented than in most narrative reviews and the clinical sections are explicit about where the evidence is insufficient, but the selection is unsystematic and single-database, nothing is appraised, the interaction evidence is the authors' own, and the treatment of harm is minimal to the point of a stated safety conclusion with no supporting data. The source can be cited for the review's own summary statements about ketamine's clinical pharmacology, for its collection of pharmacokinetic parameters by route with the primary studies named, for the cytochrome P450 interaction findings, and for its judgements about the state of the clinical evidence in February 2016. It cannot be cited as the evidence for any bioavailability figure (cite the primary study, with its sample size), for the frequency or severity of any adverse effect, or for anything about the risk of death.

key_findings.finding: Oral bioavailability of ketamine is low: the review states that 17-24% of oral racemic ketamine and 8-11% of oral S-ketamine reach the systemic circulation, citing six studies, and gives the combined range as 8-24% in the Introduction and in the Summary. The Abstract and the Key Points make the point without a number, calling oral bioavailability poor and low.
key_findings.locator: Section 1 Introduction (p. 2); Section 7.2 Oral Ketamine, 1st paragraph (p. 12); Section 9 Summary, 2nd paragraph (p. 14); Abstract (p. 1) and Key Points, 1st box (p. 2), which carry no figure
key_findings.note: The sample sizes behind these figures (3 to 12 people per study) appear only in Table 1 and never in the text.

key_findings.finding: Intramuscular bioavailability is given as approximately 93%, with the terminal plasma half-life not significantly different from that after intravenous administration, ketamine detectable in plasma after 4 minutes and peak concentrations within 5-30 minutes of injection.
key_findings.note: The figure is attached here to an intramuscular dose of 2-4 mg/kg, but the study cited for it that I read (Clements et al., 1982) gave 0.5 mg/kg and computed 93% from four participants.

key_findings.finding: Sublingual and oral ketamine are said to share poor bioavailability of 24-30%, with less norketamine formed after sublingual intake; sublingual wafer formulations are reported to vary less between people than lozenges and tablets.

Nasal bioavailability is given as approximately 45%, higher than sublingual, rectal and especially oral administration, with peak concentrations reached in 10-17 minutes and low norketamine exposure because first-pass metabolism is largely bypassed; the review adds that the amount delivered nasally is difficult to control.
key_findings.note: Cited to two studies, one of them the three-person formulation study (Yanagihara et al., 2003) whose nasal row this card's companion appraisal shows cannot rest on exactly three determinations.

key_findings.finding: Rectal bioavailability is given as approximately 30%, with a norketamine area very similar to that after a sublingual tablet, citing the same three-person study.

Disposition: a short distribution half-life of 2-4 minutes and a longer elimination half-life of 2-4 hours; plasma protein binding 10-30%; steady-state volume of distribution 160-550 L per 70 kg; systemic clearance 60-147 L/h per 70 kg, which the review describes as equalling liver blood flow and uses to explain the low oral bioavailability. The elimination half-life of S-ketamine is given as slightly longer (4-7 hours) than that of the racemate.
key_findings.locator: Section 4 Pharmacokinetics of Ketamine, 1st paragraph (p. 3), continuing on p. 6

key_findings.finding: Metabolism: ketamine is N-demethylated to norketamine, mainly by CYP3A and CYP2B6, with CYP2C9 also contributing in vitro; about 80% of ketamine is converted to norketamine, which is measurable in plasma 2-3 minutes after an intravenous bolus and peaks at 30-60 minutes; metabolites are excreted in bile and urine after glucuronidation and only traces of the parent drug appear in urine; recent work indicates norketamine is itself rapidly metabolized and may not be the main circulating metabolite.
key_findings.locator: Section 4.1 Biotransformation and Pharmacokinetic Drug-Drug Interactions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Interactions: inhibition of CYP3A by clarithromycin or grapefruit juice greatly increased exposure to oral S-ketamine; the CYP3A inducers rifampicin and St John's wort substantially reduced plasma concentrations of oral S-ketamine, with a smaller effect after intravenous administration; the CYP2B6 inhibitor ticlopidine impaired the metabolism of oral S-ketamine; itraconazole, a CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitor, had no significant interaction, which the authors attribute to concurrent action of other transporters.
key_findings.locator: Section 4.1, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 6, ends at the top of p. 7); Figures 3 and 4 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Figures 3 and 4 show mean percentage change in area and peak concentration with 95% confidence intervals but print no numbers, so no magnitude can be anchored to this review; the five underlying studies are the authors' own.

key_findings.finding: Concentration-effect relations as cited: effective concentrations for loss of consciousness 241 ng/mL (SD 90) for racemic ketamine and 111 (SD 30) for S-ketamine, and for return of consciousness 148 (SD 46) and 75 (SD 21); psychedelic effects reported from about 50 ng/mL, with intensity increasing linearly over 50-200 ng/mL; analgesia in experimental pain models above 100-160 ng/mL after intravenous racemic ketamine, and at about 40 ng/mL after oral dosing.
key_findings.locator: Section 6 Pharmacodynamics and Clinical Use of Ketamine, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The loss- and return-of-consciousness values are taken from a textbook chapter rather than a primary study.

key_findings.finding: Enantiomers: S-ketamine is described as having about four times the affinity of R-ketamine for the NMDA receptor, and is said to be postulated as about four times more potent than R-ketamine and about twice as potent as the racemate; there is no interconversion, and R-ketamine inhibits the elimination of S-ketamine, with clearance of 26.3 mL/kg/min for S-ketamine given alone, 14.8 for racemic ketamine and 18.5 for the S-enantiomer within the racemate, in ten healthy men.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Section 4.1, 1st paragraph (p. 6, for the absence of interconversion); Section 4.2, 2nd paragraph (p. 7, for the clearance figures); Section 6, 2nd paragraph (p. 9)
key_findings.note: The fourfold figure is the review's explanation of an analgesic potency difference and is attributed to a single 1992 source. It should not be confused with the separate statement in Section 5.2 (p. 8) that S-ketamine has 2 to 3 times higher affinity for opioid receptors than R-ketamine.

key_findings.finding: Oral S-ketamine produces much more metabolite than parent drug: the review reports that the S-norketamine area was 16.5 times greater than that of S-ketamine after oral dosing, that steady state is reached after the third dose without accumulation on twice-daily dosing, and that about 2.4 times more S-ketamine is needed by mouth than intravenously for the same exposure, because S-norketamine is a weaker analgesic than S-ketamine in animals.
key_findings.locator: Section 4.2, 8th paragraph (p. 8); Section 7.2 Oral Ketamine (p. 12), continuing on p. 13

key_findings.finding: Chronic postsurgical pain: two systematic reviews found that perioperative low-dose intravenous or epidural ketamine did not reduce the risk of chronic postsurgical pain, but when only intravenous studies were analysed the relative risk fell by 25% (number needed to treat 12) at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; two later randomized trials found no reduction in chronic post-thoracotomy pain.
key_findings.locator: Section 6.4.1 Ketamine in the Prevention of Chronic Pain, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Chronic and cancer pain: ketamine is reported to reduce chronic pain in several conditions in the short term, with long-term analgesic effects less well documented; in cancer pain the review states that the current evidence is insufficient to recommend ketamine as add-on therapy, citing a Cochrane review and a placebo-controlled trial of subcutaneous ketamine in 185 patients in which pain scores did not fall.
key_findings.locator: Section 6.4.2 Ketamine and Chronic Pain, 1st paragraph (p. 11); Section 6.4.3 Ketamine and Cancer Pain (p. 12); Section 9 Summary (p. 14)

key_findings.finding: Side effects and long-term safety: the review states that the safety profile of ketamine in long-term use is unclear; that chronic administration is linked to severe and persistent urinary disease including cystitis, contracted bladder and bladder wall thickening; that cognitive disturbances may affect colour perception, memory, attention, reaction time and the sense of time, with psychological dependence, in people who use ketamine long-term; and that hepatic dysfunction and hypersalivation have been reported. No frequency is given for any of these.
In the same paragraph the review states that because ketamine raises blood pressure and heart rate through sympathetic activation and preserves respiratory activity, a lethal overdose is unlikely.
key_findings.locator: Section 8 Side Effects and Limitations, 1st sentence
key_findings.note: No citation is attached to this statement and no mortality data appear anywhere in the review; it should not be used to support any claim about the risk of death.

key_findings.finding: Brain imaging as cited: an anaesthetic amount of S-ketamine increased whole-brain cerebral blood flow by 36% and a subanaesthetic amount by 13%, with the metabolic rate of oxygen and glucose virtually unaffected, so that perfusion rose most in the insula and anterior cingulate; the review also reports that monitors of anaesthetic depth do not give a reliable estimate under ketamine.
key_findings.locator: Section 6.3.2 Effects on Neurotoxicity, Neuroprotection, and Intracranial Pressure, 5th paragraph (begins p. 11); Section 6.2, last paragraph (p. 10)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 has no row attributed to reference 11, the 1982 bioavailability study, yet its first three rows reproduce exactly the values printed in Table II of that paper, which I read. The first row is attributed to reference 87 (Clements & Nimmo, 1981) and prints an area of 27.5 (1.2), a half-life of 3.1 h and norketamine values of 40 (6), 63 (23) and 35.4 (3.8); the intramuscular and oral rows are attributed to reference 10 (Grant et al., 1981) and print peaks of 243 (49) and 44 (10), times to peak of 22 (4) and 30 (5), half-lives of 2.6 and 2.9 h, an oral area of 4.8 (0.8), an oral bioavailability of 17% and norketamine values of 92 (10), 31.3 (3.8), 78 (14) and 200 (44), 36.7 (3.9), 60 (13). Every one of these is the corresponding entry of the 1982 table, with half-lives converted from minutes to hours. I have not read the two 1981 papers and cannot say whether they print the same values.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim citing this review for the intravenous, intramuscular or oral figures would be following citations to papers other than the one that prints them. Claims should cite Clements et al. (1982), where the sample sizes and the four-person bioavailability denominators are visible (see sc_clements_1982).

reporting_issues.issue: In converting those half-lives from minutes to hours, Table 1 prints the intramuscular value as 2.6 h with a standard error of 0.1. Editors' calculation against the source read for sc_clements_1982 (Table II, p. 541 of that paper, which gives 155 minutes with a standard error of 12 minutes): the standard error should be 0.2 h. The intravenous and oral conversions, 3.1 (0.1) and 2.9 (0.8), are correct.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dispersion of the intramuscular half-life is halved in the table; small, but it makes that estimate look more precise than its source does.

reporting_issues.issue: The bioavailability column of Table 1 is empty for the intramuscular row and for every row taken from the five-preparation study (reference 12), although the text gives about 93% for the intramuscular route, about 30% for the rectal and about 45% for the nasal route, and the formulation study prints bioavailability for all four of its non-injected preparations. The column is filled only for the oral row (17%), two rows from a sublingual and oral formulation study (24% each), one oral S-ketamine row (11%) and one sublingual row (29%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table does not support the three route figures the text states most prominently; a reader checking them against Table 1 would find blanks.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the time to peak for the sublingual row from reference 151 as 45 minutes with a range of 15 to 1, which cannot be a range.
reporting_issues.consequence: A printing error in one cell; that row's time to peak cannot be quoted from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 7.3 states that bioavailability is approximately 93% following an intramuscular dose of 2-4 mg/kg, citing two studies; the one I read gave 0.5 mg/kg, and the review's own Table 1 prints the intramuscular row as 0.5 mg/kg.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's text attaches a measured figure to an amount roughly five to eight times larger than the one at which it was measured, and contradicts its own table; a claim about intramuscular bioavailability should state the amount studied.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 7.4 states that the time to peak is shorter after sublingual than after oral administration (0.5 against 2 hours), citing one study; the other sublingual study in Table 1 (reference 12) gives a sublingual time to peak slightly later than its oral one (40.0 against 33.3 minutes for the (R)-enantiomer). The disagreement is not mentioned.
reporting_issues.consequence: A general statement about sublingual absorption rests on one of the two cited sources, and the review's own table contains the counter-example.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 7.2 states that peak concentrations of ketamine are reached about 40-55 minutes after ingestion, citing three sources; Table 1's oral rows give median times to peak of 42-54 minutes for oral S-ketamine but 30-33 minutes for oral racemic ketamine in one study and 120 minutes in another.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated range describes the oral S-ketamine studies, five of them by the authors' own group, and not the oral racemic studies in the same table.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 4 states that systemic clearance of 60-147 L/h per 70 kg equals liver blood flow. Editors' calculation: the hepatic blood flow of 1.53 L/min used by Clements et al. (1982) is about 92 L/h, so the cited clearance range brackets that figure rather than equalling it, its lower bound about a third below it and its upper bound about 60% above it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The argument from clearance to low oral bioavailability is sound in direction, but the range as printed includes values both well below and well above hepatic blood flow and should not be quoted as an equality.

reporting_issues.issue: The first row of Table 1 prints the amount with a comma as the decimal separator, and two later rows split the unit across lines so that a dose reads as 0.1 mg/k g.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical only, but it makes the table's amounts harder to read correctly.

reporting_issues.issue: The saved PDF is the online-first version, which carries no printed page numbers at all; the reference record gives the printed article as volume 55, issue 9, pages 1059-1077.
reporting_issues.consequence: Every anchor on this card cites the PDF's own sequential pages and says so; a reader with the printed issue will need to locate the named section rather than the page.

reporting_issues.issue: The review contradicts itself on which enantiomer produces more of the psychosis-like effects. Section 6 (p. 9) says the S(+)-enantiomer produces more auditory and visual disturbances than the R(-)-isomer, while the Abstract (p. 1) and the Summary (p. 14) say that fewer psychomimetic adverse effects have been reported with S-ketamine than with the racemate and than with R-ketamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim about how the two forms differ in subjective or psychosis-like effects may rest on a single sentence of this review; where it is cited, both statements have to be carried.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 4.1's first paragraph calls norketamine the major metabolite in humans and, three sentences later, reports that recent studies indicate it is rapidly further metabolized and is not the major metabolite in the circulation, without resolving the two.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim using this review for what the body turns ketamine into has to carry the tension rather than either half of it; the review gives no sample size or interval for either statement.
